stem: A 17-year-old who usually makes routine decisions well is considering a major elective treatment with significant long-term consequences; why should the clinician assess decision-making capacity especially carefully in this situation?

options.text: Because the gravity or seriousness of the proposed treatment is a relevant factor in competence assessment
Because any decision after age 16 no longer needs capacity assessment
Because chronic illness automatically prevents a young person from being competent
Because only parents can decide when a treatment is serious
Because seriousness matters only in emergency treatment

explanation: The correct concept is that the gravity or seriousness of the proposed treatment is a relevant factor in competence assessment. Capacity is decision-specific, so higher-stakes choices require closer attention to the young person's understanding and ability to decide.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because the seriousness of the proposed treatment is one of the factors considered when assessing competence.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because reaching 16 or 17 years does not remove the need for capacity assessment.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because chronic illness does not automatically mean a young person lacks competence.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because treatment seriousness is assessed clinically and is not decided only by parents.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because seriousness is relevant to competence assessment generally, not only in emergencies.
